stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Grades, the author argues, are a poor measure of learning and a worse motivator. Students taught to chase a letter learn to ask what will be on the test rather than what is true, and they abandon a subject the moment the grade is secured. Schools that have replaced grades with written feedback report students taking harder courses, asking more questions, and revising work they would once have discarded. The letter grade compresses a semester of thinking into a single symbol that tells a student almost nothing about what to do next. Feedback tells them exactly that, and does so while there is still time to act on it.
stimulus.text_b: Written feedback is valuable, this author agrees, and no one defends a grade as a complete account of a student. But grades do work that feedback cannot. They are comparable across teachers and schools, which lets a college or employer read a transcript from a school it has never heard of. They make it harder for bias to hide, since a vague paragraph can flatter one student and damn another without ever stating a standard. And for many students, a clear target is not a corruption of learning but the thing that gets them to the desk at all. The right reform is to improve grades, not to abolish them.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Using recovered genetic material to bring back vanished species, the author argues, is the most hopeful project in modern biology. A herd of cold-adapted elephants grazing the northern tundra could help restore grasslands that once held carbon in their soils, and the techniques developed along the way, from gene editing to artificial wombs, would serve the conservation of species that are endangered now. Extinction has always been treated as a final verdict. For the first time, it might become an appeal. The author acknowledges the project is expensive but sees in it something the field has lacked for decades: a reason for optimism.
stimulus.text_b: Resurrecting a mammoth, this author contends, would produce not a mammoth but an elephant with a few mammoth genes, raised without the mother, the herd, or the climate that made the original what it was. The money, measured in hundreds of millions, would protect dozens of species that are vanishing today and need only habitat and enforcement rather than invention. The author worries most about the lesson. If the public comes to believe that extinction is reversible, the urgency that drives conservation drains away. Hope is valuable. False hope, the author warns, is worse than none.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Companies that have tried a four-day week without cutting pay, the author reports, have mostly kept it. Employees, given a day back, cut the meetings and idle hours that had filled the fifth, and output in trials across several countries held steady while sick days fell and resignations dropped by more than a third. The author argues that the five-day week was never a law of nature; it was a compromise struck a century ago for factory labor, and knowledge work has simply inherited it. A schedule that produces the same work with less exhaustion is not a perk, the text concludes. It is the correction of a mistake.
stimulus.text_b: The four-day trials are encouraging, this author allows, but they share a flaw: the companies that volunteer for them are the ones most likely to succeed. They are small, office-based, and already flexible. A hospital, a school, or a restaurant cannot compress a week; it can only hire more people, which the trials' accounting never includes. Even in offices, the author notes, the gains came partly from cutting work that was wasteful in the first place, which a firm could do on any schedule. The text does not oppose shorter weeks. It warns that a result from firms that chose to be studied cannot be assumed to hold for firms that did not.
